notes.title: -(으)면 좋겠다
notes.text: -(으)면 좋겠어요 is the everyday way to say "I hope / I wish": 별 씨가 오면 좋겠어요 (I hope Byeol comes), 눈이 오면 좋겠다 (I wish it would snow). Koreans love the first snow (첫눈) — an old saying goes that if you're with someone at the first snow, your love will come true.

notes.title: Surprise words
notes.text: 어머! (Oh my! — used mostly by women and older people), 와! (Wow!), 음… (Um…). To welcome someone: 어서 오세요, 환영해요, or for family coming home, 잘 왔어! 몇몇 = a few, some (몇몇 사람 = some people).

scene.ko: 그날 오후, 도윤 씨가 왔어요. 두 사람이 눈을 맞추지 못해요. 분위기가 무거워요.
scene.en: That afternoon, Do-yoon arrives. The two can't look each other in the eye. The atmosphere is heavy.
b: to match, to meet (눈을 맞추다 = to look someone in the eye)

notes.title: -기를 바라다
notes.text: -기를 바라다 means "to hope that": 행복하기를 바라요 (I hope you're happy), 모두 건강하기를 바랍니다 (I hope everyone stays healthy). It's warmer and more formal than -(으)면 좋겠다 — perfect for cards and speeches.

notes.title: Size and touch
notes.text: 조그맣다 (tiny) and 커다랗다 (huge) are more vivid than 작다 and 크다. Touch: 부드럽다 (soft), 곱다 (fine, delicate, lovely). Winter street snacks: 군밤 (roasted chestnuts) and 군고구마 (roasted sweet potatoes), sold from little carts with a wonderful smell.

notes.title: -(으)ㄴ/는 김에
notes.text: -는 김에 (or -(으)ㄴ 김에 for something already done) means "while you're at it, since you're already…": 시장에 가는 김에 우유도 사 와 (since you're going to the market, grab milk too), 말이 나온 김에 (since we're on the subject). 이상형 = your ideal type — a favorite question on Korean variety shows: 이상형이 뭐예요?
